spoilers.title: Are Maya and Nao really the only ones created by a wish?
spoilers.html:
It's tinfoil hat time now. We know for a fact now that Maya and Nao are examples of characters being wished into existence.
But who is to say that there haven't been others before?

What makes Maya and Nao special? They both seem to defy certain divine laws. Maya is able to manifest a wish despite being a wish herself. Nao seems deeply connected with the gods as well, frequently travelling to other dimensions.
Now, class, who else do we know of that seems to have some divine connection and hidden powers? Hmm?
Ami. I mean, think about it. We have speculated about her knowing much more than she pretends to for the longest time. That she is similar to Maya in that regard. And now, we have the confirmation that she does have divine protection. And that she is much more powerful and knowing, at least in her current form.
And, there is even several reasons why she would have been wished into existence:
1. The most obvious one would be that Sekai wished for a daughter, possibly even specifically from Akira. Maybe it was more vague, maybe she wished for a way to be able to be with Akira, and the gods found it humorous to manifest it by her becoming pregnant by him (resulting in Kyoto).
2. I could even imagine Nozomu being the one actually wishing Ami into existence. We don't know enough about him to really speculate too much about this, but whether it would be to fulfill his wish of a daughter or to help Sekai find peace in a more roundabout way?
3. Very unlikely but maybe it was even Akira. In his case, definitely not a literal wish, but maybe also a wish to rationalize his relationship with Sekai or to "fix" her. Maybe she abandoned him in another world and he wished for her to be forced to stay with him, hence a child was born (again, Kyoto).
Now obviously this would go against the rule of only having one wish, the other one being confirmed to be Maya. But maybe...Maya was not supposed to exist because of this fact alone? Maybe it's a red herring that the issue was that Maya has had a wish fulfilled despite being a wish herself, maybe Akira started it by having been granted two wishes, becoming the target for many gods? Very far fetched, I know, just wanted to throw it out there.

One specific reason why I would find it fitting if this theory turned out to be true though is that it would create an interesting end scenario for this storyline.
Given that the main story is essentially about Akira overcoming his trauma (with everyone else's in the purity routes), it could boil down to Akira having to realize to let go off his initial wishes. He would need to face the fact that he himself has it in him to save himself, to change, that he does not need divine intervention to deal with his predatory behaviours due to trauma. Meaning that Maya should cease to exist the moment he realizes that his problems are not solved by copying Sekai but by defying her and healing from the mental wounds she has inflicted to him.
And similarly, he should have never have to wish for a justification for staying with Sekai, for interpreting their relationship as love, for forcing something into it that should not exist. In other words, that Ami should have never existed.

Thus, resulting in an endgame Ami vs. Maya, where Ami would fight to do anything to stay "alive" as a wish (assuming the logic is similar to why gods exists, as Pareidolia said: "I only exist, because you believe in me.") and create her perfect world, whereas Maya wants to stay with Akira forever, both having to ultimately learn that if they exist for Akira and truly love him, they both have to cease to exist for him to grow and become the person he needs to be to become truly happy, i.e. become a loving Dad to Himawari (assuming it's the canonical ending).

Now obviously Nao-chan would have to fit in there as well, since she bears both Ami's and Maya's eye colors, which can hardly be a coincidence, but I can't really think of anything clever here right now that would connect her to this scenario directly, especially since she is mainly connected to Kaori.

Is this likely what Selebus has in mind for the endgame, since he says he knows how it will end? Probably not. But some of the context provided so far could at least justify believing in this being a possibility.
However, in case I haven't bored you to death yet, I have another curve ball to throw at you:
Himawari also was only a wish? *cue dramatic music and Moonflare yelling in the distance*
I admit, this one is even more out there as a theory and I myself would prefer if this weren't true.
But it could make sense. During the whole of 0.53 and basically throughout the whole game itself, Hima-chan just feels....too perfect? You must have felt it too, no?

I want to explain this by Sel just being really into his own characters and actually wanting her to be this perfect, almost a Mary Sue of Lessons in Love.
But...I don't know, it could also be an epic reveal that she herself has only been a wish (most likely of course Ayane's, maybe even connected with her (not confirmed) abortion? Maybe Himawari was, as gruesome as it may be, Ayane's wish for the abortion not to take place?).
Maybe it would even go so far as, like others have already started to speculate (screenshot of her and 4 Ami's), her being in the same team as Ami?
Maybe they both fear their fate of being not needed anymore by a "cured" Akira, hence working together to direct him towards a future that is supposed to ultimately stop him from changing and just wishing to stay in this world in which both Ami and Himawari can exist.

I just can't completely detach myself from this thought, it all just seems very convenient and straightforward from here. Almost like it's a trap. The world seemed perfect, but they also basically cut themselves off from all of their friends (except for Sana). Their whole belief and happiness hinges on Himawari herself. Have they both really become their best version? Like Akira said himself, he hasn't really "deserved" this ending. They both deserve to come to their conclusion by themselves, to realize that Ayane's role is to be the mother she never truly had and for Akira to grow up and take responsibility for his actions, which essentially he didn't seem to have actively done in that world. It has been forced upon him. And the moment that both of them seem to start to develop independently from Himawari ("Let's make another baby") and Ami comes into play (Akira having to face his problems from the past) Hima-chan conveniently ends this "simulation" to not have them think about such scenarios and focus on her.

But yeah, to be fair, I don't really believe in this one myself, there's a lot of subjective interpretation forced into this. And I just don't see Sel going this far off the rails and ultimately do believe Himawari to be the intended and genuine "end goal" for this story.

Click to expand...
Ami is obviously redeemable, otherwise she wouldn't still be the most underdeveloped character according to Selebus. So I think this is a very safe bet.
That being said, the current Ami, the one we've been forced to journey with right now gives nothing in the way of rooting for her, other than wishful thinking. We can all speculate over a million things, and yet a lot of the arguments people have pulled for years to defend her have fallen with the last update. Yes, she always knew everything (or on and off at most). Yes, she was manipulating everyone. Yes, she's a cold blooded killer.

Something I've seen a lot on her defense is talking about an original Ami almost. Even in this post this appears: "she was abandoned at 15 by Akira, she was abandoned by Ayane, she can't address him as Dad, yet she remained a good aunt", did she?

We know next to nothing about who that Ami even was. Was she an Ami that lived a thousand years and fought daily to keep Akira forever imprisoned in a fake world so that he would never leave her? Cause yeah, yikes. And if she isn't, what motivated Akira and Ayane to dread her to this extent? They'd have no reason to dread an innocent Ami whose only fault is to physically resemble Sekai. So obviously there was something there.

I do sympathize with Ami to some extent though because she was fucked from the start. How do you even have any hope for a healthy relationship when she resembles and tries to emulate Sekai at every turn, even admiring her? There was just no future for the two of them ever.
Being totally honest right now, even if Akira was a lot more put together, that was an impossible situation to begin with. Let's set aside the supernatural stuff for a second and just consider the implications of having to take care of the child of your two abusers, when you yourself have no concept of either love or family, nor had a childhood to begin with. Controversial take or not, I see a very strong argument here for Ami to be adopted - Akira was just not capable of caring for a child.

But then we'd have no story, I guess.

We know next to nothing about who that Ami even was. Was she an Ami that lived a thousand years and fought daily to keep Akira forever imprisoned in a fake world so that he would never leave her? Cause yeah, yikes. And if she isn't, what motivated Akira and Ayane to
dread
her to this extent? They'd have no reason to dread an innocent Ami whose only fault is to physically resemble Sekai. So obviously there was something there.
I do sympathize with Ami to some extent though because she was fucked from the start. How do you even have any hope for a healthy relationship when she resembles and tries to emulate Sekai at every turn, even admiring her? There was just no future for the two of them ever.
Being totally honest right now, even if Akira was a lot more put together, that was an impossible situation to begin with. Let's set aside the supernatural stuff for a second and just consider the implications of having to take care of the child of your two abusers, when you yourself have no concept of either love or family, nor had a childhood to begin with. Controversial take or not, I see a very strong argument here for Ami to be adopted - Akira was just not capable of caring for a child.
But then we'd have no story, I guess.

The part that really gets me is that Ami isn't even allowed to call Akira "Dad". No matter what she did, that just feels vindictive.
As for the Ami in Sensei's world: nope, sorry, still not buying that it's that simple. The Ami in Chapter 3 wasn't a cold-blooded killer and I will die on this hill.

Hi everyone, I took a break from LiL and the forum for a couple of months until the new update dropped, but since then I’ve tried to catch up at least the last 30 pages. This update was really good — it’s been since… ever that I felt so emotionally invested in a story and its characters.


About the world and the wishes… it’s all quite confusing. What I thought to be a world inspired by DnD’s Ravenloft setting, the Domains of Dread and their Darklords (which I still think it is, at least as a basic premise of inspiration), is instead revealed to be a bureaucratic mess of a universe, where all the figures of power are less outright evil and more just insane, desperate gods willing to do anything to keep existing. (As I slowly replayed the game, I realized the first DnD session we see literally has the standard introduction to any Ravenloft campaign: “You are taken by the mists from different realms and find yourselves together in a new world,” with Sensei even implicitly acknowledging it’s something he can relate to).


About Ami: I think Ami is not irredeemable as a character, but I do think the current iteration of her is. We’ve seen her character kill in two different realities, and we know she’s done it more times before. We’ve seen her being negatively influenced by Sekai’s ghost (or in person); she’s becoming more unhinged and villain-like with each update, and she has untreated psychopathic tendencies that have gone unacknowledged for far too long in her life.

I think i remember this isn’t even the first time she’s threatened to kill Sensei (or at least pondered violence while talking to no one - probably Sekai or a god), since she had that mental breakdown when she cut her hair, but i’m not sure.

To me, it seems her real mental changes began when she started reading her mom’s poems in Chapter 2 (like in the “My Life With You” event). Before that, either she didn’t retain all her memories from past cycles, or she was simply so used to seeing Sensei reset each time and to easily seduce him again and again. Once Sensei stopped resetting and began to truly progress with other girls, she became increasingly unstable and unable to keep up the act anymore.

Anyway, I actually think the end of the current route, the Harem Route, can’t be possible while Ami, or at least this iteration of Ami exists. My opinion is that the end of the Harem Route will show a world without Ami and without resets.
In such an ending, Akira will be able to finally “complete” his harem at the cost of Ami (or at least this version of her). But without the resets to erase time-progression issues, everything will continue into the Dark Route, which will take place in a more “normal” world. Himawary herself said so, the time of this ever-resetting world is coming to an end. Still, i'm not so convinced beacuse i can't see Sel completely remove a character for the whole Dark Route.


Himawari’s pocket world: I like to imagine Himawari’s pocket world simply a world where Maya never existed, with the progression of thing going as (all of this is my imagination going, nothing with solid bases on):

  • Maya was never there to give solace to Sensei -> Sensei finds solace in Ami much sooner than the current timeline.
  • Sensei keeps screwing his students, then falls in love with Ayane, Ayane gets pregnant and Sensei finds in his new daughter something he can love more than Ami, mirroring Sekai’s events when Ami was born.
  • Sensei and Ami keep seeing eachother, but keep their relationship secret to everyone, again mirroring his story with Sekai.
  • Ayane finds out about them / Sensei tells the truth to Ayane many years later, he has to make a decision - to choose between Ayane and Himawari and Ami – He choose the first.
  • Time passes until the events of Himawari’s pocket world are realized.
Also, i think Himawari will be born in the Dark Route world, the linear timeline world, and chose her path after seeing her dad offing himself due to events that still have to happen in this timeline, Akira's future suicide was implied too many times to not have an important relevance in the story.

Many ways for Maya's wish to go wrong, but I have ideas.

She wanted a world where she could share Sensei with Ami, but instead she is in love, and want to not share anymore.

Second idea I have. What if Maya wishes for a world with no death? This is why resets happen so many times, because people die and makes everything reset. People said before they think that Chinami dies for reset, but another reset happens right when Ami disappears, and dies. Mini reset happens in Bluejay. Something happens to break the wish, maybe the gods getting bored, which makes Makoto Dad die, and the school collapse, because world, and wish is breaking apart.

Third idea I have. Maya wishes for a world where Sensei is alive, but she blames herself for him dying. She is not allowed to fall in love with Sensei, because in her wish she cannot love Sensei, or he will die.

Sorry I am not as clever as other people here, but I have read everything here for a long time, and every time I am excited to read people's clever ideas. I like Deskel, Aramaug, and many others clever ideas a lot.

Hello again folks, I don't chime in very often but the latest update has gotten my attention once again. In particular, I find the discussion about the "redemption" of Ami fascinating. "She's gone too far!" (or) "She'll come around in the end!". As if we, the spectators strapping ourselves to the narrative rails of a madman, have any say in the matter.


What makes sapient life so valuable? It's ability to react? It's ability to change over time? It's agency over it's actions? It's awareness of itself?

In my view, what makes a beings life valuable to humans is that due to the shared experience and social nature of the species, the feelings and experiences of other organisms can be and often are as much of a part of an individuals life as it's own. This explains why geographical, ideological and economic disparity can create the opposite effect, alienating those organisms to such a degree they become indifferent to each other, or even hostile to the point of seeking their destruction.

This means that the majority of humans subscribe to their own personal ethical bubble that determines who and what their ethics calls for them to defend and conversely, who to disregard or oppose.

In other words, beings land within or without the ethical bubble of humans based on the parity of experiences each individual has with the other. You cannot value another being enough to sacrifice for them if you cannot understand them. This doesn't require linguistic communication, just a shared rhythm and limitations. A shared suite of daily needs and wants. We all eat, we all sleep and we all (want to) fuck. The difference between a peer and a pet is a disparity in agency and communication, not the fundamental rules they live by.

---------

So, with that in mind, there's something that I always find very relevant in the realm of Denpa and Lovecraftian works. Quite often, typically abhorrent and unjust actions can become benign or even preferable when the context around those actions is sufficiently alien.

By the end of a quality lovecraftian experience, you have been dragged into the realm of madness alongside some other sapience and you see the world through their eyes. What was alien is now accepted, and what was normal is now alarming, causing threat or disgust or pain or sorrow or any number of other negative reactions. Living an existence with an entirely different set of limitations and rules is the most fundamental feature of the unknowable horrors of eldritch and the occult, and from that fundamental stems the true nature of the danger posed by something so otherworldly.

It doesn't know, it doesn't understand and it doesn't care.

---------

I submit that Eternal Ami is an eldritch god. A being that has existed in such an impossible and alien world that she is the sole being of her kind. She no longer connects with the petty simplicity within the needs and wants of Kumon-Mi residents, nor could any bound by the rules of the resets even dream to understand her. Whether this comes with unfathomable powers is irrelevant, her godhood is earned by living on separate layer of reality.

What we see is the most isolated being in the universe begging and pleading and clawing and scraping and trying everything to bring something, anything into her world so she doesn't have to face it alone. When that fails, existence itself loses all meaning as you lose connection to every aspect of the old world you used to live in. While Eternal Ami persists in this form, redemption is an irrelevant concern. She is neither worthy nor unworthy of redemption, she is beyond the reach of judgement itself.

Eventually, finally, maybe... She will either drag us into her world or fall into ours. Only then can our limited scales contain her long enough to weigh her actions.

Or perhaps we will meet her in madness on our own...

Ami no Uta
What makes sapient life so valuable? It's ability to react? It's ability to change over time? It's agency over it's actions? It's awareness of itself?
In my view, what makes a beings life valuable to humans is that due to the shared experience and social nature of the species, the feelings and experiences of other organisms can be and often are as much of a part of an individuals life as it's own. This explains why geographical, ideological and economic disparity can create the opposite effect, alienating those organisms to such a degree they become indifferent to each other, or even hostile to the point of seeking their destruction.
This means that the majority of humans subscribe to their own personal ethical bubble that determines who and what their ethics calls for them to defend and conversely, who to disregard or oppose.
In other words, beings land within or without the ethical bubble of humans based on the parity of experiences each individual has with the other. You cannot value another being enough to sacrifice for them if you cannot understand them. This doesn't require linguistic communication, just a shared rhythm and limitations. A shared suite of daily needs and wants. We all eat, we all sleep and we all
(want to)
fuck. The difference between a peer and a pet is a disparity in agency and communication, not the fundamental rules they live by.
---------
So, with that in mind, there's something that I always find very relevant in the realm of Denpa and Lovecraftian works. Quite often, typically abhorrent and unjust actions can become benign or even preferable when the context around those actions is sufficiently alien.
By the end of a quality lovecraftian experience, you have been dragged into the realm of madness alongside some other sapience and you see the world through their eyes. What was alien is now accepted, and what was normal is now alarming, causing threat or disgust or pain or sorrow or any number of other negative reactions. Living an existence with an entirely different set of limitations and rules is the most fundamental feature of the unknowable horrors of eldritch and the occult, and from that fundamental stems the true nature of the danger posed by something so otherworldly.
It doesn't know, it doesn't understand and it doesn't care.
---------
I submit that Eternal Ami is an eldritch god. A being that has existed in such an impossible and alien world that she is the sole being of her kind. She no longer connects with the petty simplicity within the needs and wants of Kumon-Mi residents, nor could any bound by the rules of the resets even dream to understand her. Whether this  comes with unfathomable powers is irrelevant,  her godhood is earned by living on separate layer of reality.
What we see is the most isolated being in the universe begging and pleading and clawing and scraping and trying everything to bring something, anything into her world so she doesn't have to face it alone. When that fails, existence itself loses all meaning as you lose connection to every aspect of the old world you used to live in. While Eternal Ami persists in this form, redemption is an irrelevant concern. She is neither worthy nor unworthy of redemption, she is beyond the reach of judgement itself.
Eventually, finally, maybe... She will either drag us into her world or fall into ours. Only then can our limited scales contain her long enough to weigh her actions.
Or perhaps we will meet her in madness on our own...
Click to expand...
tl;dr: "Ami is an eldritch horror."
I can agree to that bottom line.

Yeah I got what you meant, I just think that what we do see on the screen implies otherwise too strongly.

For example as I said, Ami has never been alone. We have no reason to think she pre-dates Maya - quite the contrary, since we now know that the world is a product of Maya's wish it makes sense to assume she's the one with the longest memory span and most consistent memory retention. Ami seemingly has to facilitate her own retention with some sort of trickery and/or outside influence, ergo it doesn't make much sense to me to assume her personality has warped this way out of loneliness when she's always had at least one being who could share in her situation - a being who, seemingly, she has also mostly chosen to treat the same way she treats the regular people she sees as dolls (although admittedly we can't say that for certain, for all we know they could've been genuine friends at one point).

I feel like your description her would be more apt for Maya Prime, honestly. She openly lamented the pain of not being able to grow and of being stuck in an infinite loop whilst Ami has expressed that eternity with her uncle is just Heaven to her. The whole rub here is that Ami likes where she is and has no desire for it to end. Of course, one could certainly argue those feelings are the result of dealing with the situation for so long and speculate that she might not have felt that way initially or for a long time but I'm just not really gonna assume that until it's implied or exposited somewhere.

Since this topic started with morality I'd also like to point out that despite her many years Maya Prime was still a human being - she had a high tolerance for weird shit and could be somewhat callous but she still seemed to possess basic human morals and a human perception of right and wrong, which makes it difficult for me to justify giving Ami Prime a pass on the basis that she's too alien to be judged at this point.

Just in case I'm coming across wrong here I'm not trying to be dismissive or argumentative here or something, just saying why I don't agree right now with this particular viewpoint on Ami. I do find the subject interesting though, I've thought about it quite a bit since I first read the event where Makoto speculates a bit on the impact of time on morality.

Hi everyone, I have some other ideas to share after some insomnia-fueled thoughts from last night.

Two Wishes, One Person: If every person can have only one wish granted, and Maya, who was born from an incredibly selfish wish by Akira, somehow managed to make a completely selfless wish, something meant for Akira and only him, then maybe in this heavenly bureaucratic mess of a world, that second wish existance was seen as incompatible with the first one.
Since it was a wish made by a wish, maybe the system interpreted it as Akira effectively having two wishes granted — which isn’t allowed.

This could have caused both wishes to malfunction: Akira could no longer enjoy his first wish (Maya’s function), because it became “locked out” from him (again, one wish per person), without Maya being fully erased, like, maybe erasing Akira's memories about everything was just easier. (Maybe deleting a wished person is more complex than simply excluding them.)
At the same time, Akira found himself trapped inside Maya’s selfless wish.
I won’t speculate too deeply about what exactly Maya wished for. I’ve seen some theories some of you made in previous posts, but i still have no idea, personally, the only thing that makes sense to me so far is some kind of world where Sensei can have some sort of easier life, even without Maya.

Maya’s wish created a kind of paradox. The first wish (her existence and function) could no longer function because it was overridden by the second wish — her wish made for Akira.
This would explain why, after Maya Prime reset, Sensei could go back to have sex with New Maya: because she wasn’t perceived anymore as Akira’s wish. She still was, in truth, but Akira didn’t think of her that way — and in this chaotic, paperwork-driven universe, that misperception was enough.
Now that Akira has realized New Maya is still Maya, and that he’s in love with her, things might shift again. We’ll see in the future updates i guess.

Niki’s convenient existence: Regarding Himawari telling Sensei to be realistic about Niki’s existence — how she seems too convenient for this world — I think Niki herself might be the result of a wish.
A wish made by a Niki who, after leaving Sensei to pursue her idol career, found herself wishing for another chance with him, even though she knew it was too late.
It was too late for her original self, in her original worlf, maybe, but not for the Wish-Niki who appeared in Akira’s world. That version of her had the perfect setup to try and try again, to stay with Sensei this time.
Another wish made by one person but “enjoyed” by their wish-copy, if “enjoyed” is even the right word for what Niki is going through right now in the story.

Moonflare said:
While I find this funny, I think you're missing a few things.

The gods don't think Maya is wrong, the company is simply trying to understand how this took place, since it shouldn't be possible for a wish to have a wish of her own. They torture Maya because they ran out of ideas thousands of years ago. At this point, any sort of idea to get a different reaction from her is fair game.

Himawari's reasoning for pointing at Maya and Ami is far different. Our Akira is not the Akira of Maya's wish world. He's an outsider, maybe the Akira that Maya made the wish for.

And Himawari, for obvious reasons, wants him to escape (because he's not from there in the first place). Ami wants him to stay (for whatever reason - since it's unclear if she even distinguishes between Akiras), and Maya Prime wants him to stay because he's (possibly) the actual Akira that also should never have been there, but is the one she wishes to be.

In this sense, both of them are adversaries to the goal of getting Himawari's Akira out of there, yes. The gods/company could care less.
Click to expand...
Well, there is (at least) one problem with Himawari's goals that doesn't seem to make much sense.

Apparently, Akira and Ayane will be sent back to where they are meant to be, if the world gets cleansed:
(Chapter 4 Ayane 'Aomori' Event)

So, if Himawari isn't the reason the world is falling apart, then simply doing nothing should get her what she wants. However, she clearly feels the need to interfere.

This suggests that her actual goal is different. Presumably, she just wants to create a world where Ayane and Akira create her and live happily ever after. (Nothing and no one else matters)

To accomplish something even remotely like this, she seems to believe that Maya cannot exist:
(Chapter 4 'Behind The Scenes' Main Event)
Because with Maya around, it would be extremely unlikely for Akira to end up with Ayane. (Frankly, I don't see why he'd end up with Ayane if Maya doesn't exist either, but Himawari is optimistic...)

There's also how Maya may exist where Akira is meant to be:
(Chapter 4 'Behind The Scenes' Main Event)
Which isn't something that Himawari wants to be true for obvious reasons.

But to get rid of Maya would probably require stopping Ami, who is more or less safeguarding Maya's wish and this world. So, while they want nothing to do with Himawari or gods, Himawari needs to get rid of them to get what she wants.

There's also seemingly another and potentially way bigger problem...

Where Akira, and possibly whoever else, is meant to be, may no longer even exist. Terminal 22, which Nao-chan claims is Akira's home:
(Chapter 4 Nao-chan 'A House Near a Lake (The Same Place as Always)' Event)
Is apparently just straight up gone, according to Yasu's implications:
(Chapter 3 (not 4) 'Happy Memories' Main Event)

This might explain why Himawari is unable to find out where Akira (and Ayane) belong. It could be because it's simply gone.

In that case then Himawari's plans are screwed and if this world, presumably Terminal 23, collapses or gets cleansed then everyone within it may be screwed. Or at least homeless, assuming they don't end up in a world like The Pareidolia Mall or in Himawari's wish-world, etc.

I don't think Ayane's epilogue was supposed to suggest that the "real world" Akira will end up like in this wish world. It's essentially Himawari's wish, so it's yet another parallel universe or wish world, however you want to phrase it, in which everything goes according to what's in Himawari's best interest. At least that's what she claims.

We don't really know the real order of actions from the past, who the real world Akira is, we can only speculate.
At this point, we cannot be sure of anyone else not also being a wish of someone existing in this world.

Moonflare and DeSkel already provided good theories, but they are just that, theories.
Personally I'm not convinced yet that everything is as it seems to be, the game is full of unreliable narrators, gods have been proven to misinform and misguide just for the fun of it or to escalate situations. Is everything that Himawari is saying actually true?
What exactly have been Prime Maya's and Ami's true intentions?
What exactly made Akira wish for Maya?
And why did Maya wish for this world to exist and how did she do it in the first place?

I already theorized that Niki, at least as we know her in this world, is not real either, especially since Himawari hinted at that already. And it may as well turn out that the same applies to others.
There is a suspicious amount of fatherless characters in the story, it would not be totally crazy to think that maybe the "real" or "past" Akira was involved and this world is based on his or someone's wish to have him get the chance to see his alleged daughters grow up and help them out with their traumas and make them love him (guess he should have been careful about phrasing here) or something like that. Many stories are based on this sort of dilemma.

At the end of the day we don't know what's hiding in Sel's sick mind, but I'm curious to get some answers to the many questions there still are.

What gatcha game is this Ciri Rawiyah character from?
Click to expand...
"Sword of Convallaria".
It is a free tactics rpg gacha game. The gacha aspect is quite tame tbh, I have a lot of high tier summons and never paid anything.
And I quite like the art as well
What drew me in was that it has quite an extensive single player campaign which is separate from the gacha almost entirely. So, basically, you get a full single player game for free. It is a fantasy medieval rpg that you can restart to get different endings.
Then I stayed for the gacha later, but they're two separate modes of play. You can use the gacha characters in single-player mode, but it is not required.

The combat itself is a tactics rpg, that you can also set to auto-battle on/off at any point.
Funnily enough, witcher 3 is coming to convallaria later this month:
All that aside, if you like that sort of tactics single player game, maybe give it a try? It's free after all. The story itself leaves a bit to be desired tbh, and I think that if they made an actual single player game and sold it, rather than make a gacha out of it, it would have been better.

Nevertheless, it's sort of on the same level as Triangle Strategy, but again, this one's free.
tldr; if you like games like final fantasy tactics and triangle strategy, give it a try because there's a full single player game mode there, separate from the gacha. It's free, so you don't really lose anything.

Good moment to remind people that "The Last Sovereign" is also free, and finally completed on steam (25% of adult scenes art missing though).

What exactly is the Green Route and Red Route. How do I know which one I took? Does Green mean Good Choice and Red Bad?
Click to expand...
On a more serious note, when we say red route or green route, we refer to the event gallery in the game and whether the event has played out (green with check mark) or whether it has been missed (red with strike-through text).

Yes, these are Ami events from my red route save because Ami sucks (except she doesn't get to suck her uncle)
So a green route save is when all events have been triggered and none have been missed, any missed event would mean it's now on the red route.

Think of it as canon vs. non-canon, because Sel has been very frank about his opinion of anyone electing to not trigger any scenes in his game. If it were to him, this game would be entirely kinetic and there wouldn't even be the option to miss events (I guess except for happy events that he likes to hide so much).

Similarly, there are certain flags that could trigger events in the future, so missing those could also be considered "not optimal play" for anyone who is intent on staying on the green route.

I wouldn't put it past Sel if he just weren't able to give a clear and satisfying answer to all of those kinds of questions at the end of the day, simply because it can get quite complicated and it's easy to mess something up in terms of continuity and plot integrity.

At this point I would not assume too much, there is some deliberate omission of facts still, we can't know for sure how certain things work, especially if it has been shown that some things just happen at the whim of one god or another.

Again, this is probably something that can get really complicated and I'm not 100% certain Sel even intends to clearly explain this at any point in the future.
But I myself see the fact that Maya refers to this Akira as the true Akira in relation to the resets that keep resetting people's memories. And I think it is established that the resets don't reset the world itself (it is referred to as one and the same world by the custodians, a world that existed for a very long time but just resets far more often than usual) but the inhabitants.

posts.content_html_raw:
On the topic of what the hell is going on with Ami:

Personally, I'm leaning towards all the killing being akin to sacrificing to a god for benefits. Including committing suicide, in at least Ami's case (maybe Makoto's):
The World Itself which may also be known as The Sky, which possibly takes Sekai's form, possibly created Nao in Ami's image, and is possibly the illegal god/thing who's protecting Ami, has been implied to be sadistic and to desire to cover others in it's hatred:
(Chapter 3 Makoto 'White Oak Doors' Lust Event)
And watch them suffer:
(Chapter 3 Yasu 'The River Styx' Event)
This god/thing could potentially want Ami to cause suffering and kill others for it's amusement, and in exchange, keeps her, among other things, going. Sacrifices for boons.

Or potentially, Ami could be keeping it content so that it doesn't go overboard on causing suffering.

Eitherway it'd fit Ami's caretaker title, and why she ranted about what she's been doing for Sensei that he couldn't know about, on top of why she claims she's just good at things and has no real powers.

There's also how Ami has referenced the Sky:
(Chapter 4 'God Of Light' Main Event)
And how Yasu thoroughly fears it's mighty tendrils:
(Chapter 3 Yasu 'The River Styx' Event)

Overall: It's not clear, but surely there is more to Ami than just being kill crazy. She is far too two-faced to be so one dimensional.

And I struggle to see why else New Maya leaving in one piece isn't really up to her apparently:
(Chapter 4 Maya 'Right As Rain' Event)

She also literally went from threatening to kill Ayane and Sensei to immediately trying to help Ayane with her headache, just last update.

That doesn't sound like someone who really just wants to murder everything, especially since she claims to be the only one that's real, while consistently showing that she cares for others that are in pain.
---
Also, off topic, but I am hoping that Ami will finally show Sensei the pics of her and Maya next update. That'll be an interesting situation after what Sensei has just found out about both, and Ami seems to have plans for Christmalloween.

CrimsonSand12 said:
So I was thinking about it and if someone has an explanation I would love to hear it as I probably missed something. Why is Himawari so attached to Ayane? I understand that's her mom, but if the world as we know it was a wish created by Maya and Akira apparently is "actually him". Would that not imply that the Ayane we see is just a wish construction and not her actual mom? Meddling with Akira makes sense but not so much with Ayane given the new information, but again I probably missed something.
Click to expand...
This is actually a good question but I don't know if Selly has been discrete enough about the matter to answer this , but for now let's give him some benefits of the doubt and see if we can run our imagination.

Maybe Himiwari doesn't have the need to differentiate Ayanes across different timelines/worlds. Unlike her actual dad who probably got "transferred to other worlds/timelines", the rest of Ayanes Himawari might encounter are instead, "exact duplicates of her mom spawned from third party wishes". I won't say these duplicates are completely indistinguishable, but I do think distinguishing them are not very meaningful if 1) all Ayanes behave and act the same as the mom she knows, and 2) when we are in a setting where everyone can make wishes and create worlds, resulting in possibly billions of barely distinguishable parallel timelines filled with billions of highly similar Ayanes, with one being just as real as the next. With that, I'd say it means very little for our sweetheart Himawari to deliberately keep her distance.

Under a more extreme speculation, however, Himawari might even have extra incentives to view our Ayane just as her actual mom. Let's say, shortly after an unsuccessful confiding, our pregnant Ayane made a wish before reset3 hit. She wished for a future where both Akira and she were able to handle Ayane's pregnancy a lot more differently, leading to the Himawari we now know. Thus, even if our Ayane technically isn't her actual mom, she would still be the source of her existence but perhaps no longer in a strict causality sense, and this would give Himawari enough reasons to view our Ayane just like her actual mom.

We also can't rule out that maybe our Ayane really IS her actual mom but in the past, who just hasn't broken out of Kumon-mi and eventually married Akira. This, however, would require to think about too many other technicality plus continuity questions which will not have answers for quite some time so I am putting a pin in it.

You mean the Almond Eye comment? Well, in racehorsing Fillies and Mares are considered less desirable than Colts and Stallions because they tend to show lower performance and they are less versatile when it comes to breeding (A Male can breed hundreds of times in a year while a Female can only be pregnant once a year) so even if the performance gap isn't that far apart, you'd still choose to focus on a Male Horse because if it does become successful, it can leave a lot more stronger descendants.

The thing is that Horses have a lesser practical gap when it comes to physical differences between Male and Female compared to Humans (Strictly for racing)
The average Stallion can have a bigger muscular mass to the average Mare compared to the difference between the Average Man and Woman for example, but the physical differences specifically for Horse Racing are less practical, so Mares are sometimes capable of beating the most elite Stallions.
This is why Almond Eye's achievements are so impressive, she is the Japanese Horse that won the most G1 Turf races (which is the highest tier there is) and she was the Greatest Mare by FAR.
(I think she's the only Mare in the Top 10, but she's at the TOP)

I guess this also goes to show that Himawari is also the greatest

In the last update, things got really strange when adult Sana was alone with Sensei. Her whole demeanor changes and she hints at knowing things she shouldn't. She asks pointed open-ended questions to get him thinking about uncomfortable truths, and yet she keeps smiling the whole time. She toys with him, giving only a trickle of information when she clearly could tell him more.

Does that sound like anyone else we know? How about if I show you a visual comparison?
While it sounds tinfoil, my best guess is that it wasn't Sana saying these things, it was Tsubasa speaking through her. That leaves big questions of how and why, but first let's take a more detailed look at the weird things she says.
The main content of the conversation is Sana hinting that she knows the true nature of this world. Specifically, she implies that:
  • There are multiple worlds.
  • Different girls "win" and end up with Akira in other worlds.
  • Sensei went from his own world to this future in an instant, instead of living through the fifteen years.
Technically it's possible that Sana knows nothing and is just talking about other possible worlds in a figurative sense. We can safely reject this idea, though, because of just how much is off in this scene. Selebus also has Akira notice what's happening and bring it up again later, emphasizing to the reader that Sana said something meaningful.
She says a few other things which can be interpreted as hints that this isn't coming from Sana.
  1. She raises a question of "who am I?", which might be asking whether Sensei is the same person in this world, but might also be about herself - is she Sana, or is she someone else speaking through her?
  2. She denies knowing things when Sensei asks, but notice that she doesn't claim total ignorance, only that she knows no more than she did "back then", i.e. in Sensei's world. Since we have to accept that she does know something now, that means either she's lying or she's someone who knew stuff "back then" as well (i.e. not Sana).
  3. She talks about rules that are constantly changing. Himawari has to follow (or not) the seemingly arbitrary rules of the corporation when interacting with Sensei and his world, and I think other narrators have talked about rules as well.
If it's Tsubasa speaking, these things make sense. At the very least she already knows about multiple worlds (she mentions them to Himawari), and she is very likely to be one of the narrators who have to follow a set of rules.
As soon as Sana is alone with Sensei, she begins acting weird, starting with her very first sentence: she claims that Sensei and Ayane were in love when she met them.
This definitely wasn't true in Sensei's world. Ayane said she fell in love with Sensei when she was 11, but before the events of the game he only treated her like a daughter. He never responded to her obvious flirting or gave any sign that he was sexually attracted to her. I don't remember when Sana met them, but it was definitely by the start of high school, at which point this was still the case. Even during the game, Sensei doesn't start to feel any actual love for Ayane until sometime later in Chapter 2, IIRC.

The simplest explanation for Sana's comment is that it's true specifically for this Sana because Sensei fell in love with Ayane earlier in Himawari's wish world. Maybe because he inevitably pursued a different loli girlfriend in a world with no Maya (ew) or because it was part of Himawari's wish (double ew). But even if Sel decided that was true in this world, I doubt he'd reveal it this way. Why leave it so ambiguous? Why use it to start the Sana Knows Things conversation?

A more tinfoil explanation is that someone else is speaking through Sana, and they're either mistaken about Sana's past or are speaking from their own perspective. That doesn't fit Tsubasa perfectly, as she met Sensei before he loved Ayane, but it might if you interpret it as if/when she met the two of them together (she's been in the same room as Ayane, but I don't think we've seen them speak to each other).
We've already seen that Sana and Tsubasa said this line in different events while adopting extremely similar poses.
The visual similarities are enough to know this isn't coincidence, but the "cat got your tongue" idiom is unusual as well. Selebus has only had characters say it three times before: once by a voice in Sensei's head (probably Pareidolia) and twice by Tsubasa.

Context: Pareidolia (or some other entity) taunts Sensei about Maya Prime right after she goes pop on the roof.

Context: Sensei says he's a danger around Tsukasa and implies he's a pedophile, and Tsubasa brings up his past and fakes that she's going to call the police.

Context: Tsubasa imitates Sekai in order to dredge up Sensei's trauma, making him easier to manipulate.
Something occurred to me while I was putting together this post: it's possible that in all these cases the "cat" is a deliberate reference to Maya (the stray cat). The first one definitely is. The second one is in the context of Akira's past and how he might abuse a wizard, so a Maya reference makes total sense. The third one is less obvious, but Sensei's guilt over what he did to Maya is part of his trauma, so Tsubasa might bring that up along with the Sekai stuff. Of course this requires Tsubasa to know about Maya, but why not when she knows intimate details about his relationship with Sekai and has used her connections to investigate his past?

So why does "Sana" use the same phrase in this scene? Well, she says it in the middle of a discussion of other possible worlds where different girls end up with Akira, so maybe she wants him to think about a world where he ends up with Maya. On the face of it, it's kind of ridiculous that a reference so subtle could have any effect, but it might have worked: later that night, Sensei thinks about his conversation with Sana, and then almost immediately afterward he thinks about being with Maya instead of Ayane.

(That's not what she was doing, but he's rationalizing it that way so he can dismiss it.)
Maybe the roof scene was so traumatic that it primed him to think of Maya whenever he heard "cat got your tongue" from then on.
Some of these oddities are better explained if it's Tsubasa talking, but would she really be able to speak through Sana? I think the idea is less ridiculous than it seems on the surface, even if we don't know the specifics of how it happened.
I'm going to throw out some guesses, but this is all very speculative. These probably weren't the most important concerns to Selebus - I'm guessing he started with what he wanted Sensei to hear, and only then figured out the most reasonable messenger and how to make it happen; he didn't start from an idea of Sana/Tsubasa/whoever wanting to say these things.

We know (or at least highly suspect) Tsubasa is a narrator (see post 1, post 2, post 3). As part of that role, she describes characters' thoughts, which means she can get inside their heads to at least some extent. As narrator she may be able to influence thoughts as well, such as when she spoke directly to Rin about a ticking clock and Rin heard it, or how she was the first to suggest the idea of Sensei becoming a god before he started thinking about it himself.

I admit there's a big leap between subconscious influence and total control of thoughts/speech, but there may be precedent for a narrator putting words in a girl's mouth: in "T is for Time" Makoto said some uncharacteristic things which echoed earlier narration. The other world's Sana could be even easier to influence since she's a clone.

During the time that Sensei and Ayane were in Himawari's world*, Tsubasa's body was apparently unconscious back in Kumon-mi, waiting to be killed and dismembered by Ami. But if you think about it, it's likely there's something more complex going on. The RAS's knowledge lets them stay awake during resets, so shouldn't the narrator who knows even more than them be able to do the same? Plus, we see Shiori preparing to reset Tsubasa, but we know she somehow avoids getting mind-wiped.

I had a thought: maybe Tsubasa is able to retain her memories because her mind isn't in her body when she gets reset. Sensei has the ability to mentally slip between worlds, ending up in the mind of another world's Akira. Maybe Tsubasa can do the same thing, but can enter minds other than just the other world's Tsubasa thanks to her narrator abilities.

[*] (off topic) I'm confused by the timeline: four months passed in Himawari's wish world. Himawari spent the same amount of time looking for her parents, so time wasn't moving faster there than the rest of the multiverse. But was Kumon-mi really in limbo for that long? I doubt Ami was rampaging for four months or that the corporation waited four months to send in a custodian to reset the world. And what was that whole deal with Himawari needing to keep her parents safe from a factory reset? What changed to prevent that?

So here is my extremely speculative theory of what happened:
  1. The reset starts. Tsubasa slips to Himawari's wish world, either because she knows Sensei will be there or just because she wants to learn more about her new ally (Himawari).
  2. Tsubasa seizes an oppurtunity to talk to Sensei through Sana, giving him cryptic hints so he doesn't become complacent in the idea of a monogamous future with Ayane. (Whatever Tsubasa's goals are, she's been throwing Tsukasa at Sensei to try and get him to embrace his inner predator. Himawari's wish is the antithesis to that.)
  3. Sensei returns to Kumon-mi and the custodians do their work. Shiori resets Tsubasa's body, but it's an empty vessel while her mind is elsewhere.
  4. After the custodians are finished, Tsubasa slips back into her restored body.
Of course, whether this would actually let her avoid the mind wipe depends on metaphysical questions about what it means to slip and whether your mind is still tied to your original brain. We don't have the answer to those, so it's at least possible.

One strike against this theory: it doesn't explain the adult Sana in "Four Letter Words" who recognizes Sensei and tells him she loves him. It would be cleaner if the two weird adult Sana scenes had the same explanation, but for now I don't see a way to tie them together.


I did briefly consider the possibility that it's Maya Prime speaking through Sana instead of Tsubasa, but in the "Infinite Joy" scene I can't see any reflection of Maya in her demeanor the way that I can with Tsubasa.

spoilers.title: 'When I met you'
spoilers.html:
As soon as Sana is alone with Sensei, she begins acting weird, starting with her very first sentence: she claims that Sensei and Ayane were in love when she met them.
This definitely wasn't true in Sensei's world. Ayane said she fell in love with Sensei when she was 11, but before the events of the game he only treated her like a daughter. He never responded to her obvious flirting or gave any sign that he was sexually attracted to her. I don't remember when Sana met them, but it was definitely by the start of high school, at which point this was still the case. Even during the game, Sensei doesn't start to feel any actual love for Ayane until sometime later in Chapter 2, IIRC.

The simplest explanation for Sana's comment is that it's true specifically for this Sana because Sensei fell in love with Ayane earlier in Himawari's wish world. Maybe because he inevitably pursued a different loli girlfriend in a world with no Maya (ew) or because it was part of Himawari's wish (double ew). But even if Sel decided that was true in this world, I doubt he'd reveal it this way. Why leave it so ambiguous? Why use it to start the Sana Knows Things conversation?

A more tinfoil explanation is that someone else is speaking through Sana, and they're either mistaken about Sana's past or are speaking from their own perspective. That doesn't fit Tsubasa perfectly, as she met Sensei before he loved Ayane, but it might if you interpret it as if/when she met the two of them together (she's been in the same room as Ayane, but I don't think we've seen them speak to each other).

spoilers.title: 'Cat got your tongue?'
spoilers.html:
We've already seen that Sana and Tsubasa said this line in different events while adopting extremely similar poses.
The visual similarities are enough to know this isn't coincidence, but the "cat got your tongue" idiom is unusual as well. Selebus has only had characters say it three times before: once by a voice in Sensei's head (probably Pareidolia) and twice by Tsubasa.

Context: Pareidolia (or some other entity) taunts Sensei about Maya Prime right after she goes pop on the roof.

Context: Sensei says he's a danger around Tsukasa and implies he's a pedophile, and Tsubasa brings up his past and fakes that she's going to call the police.

Context: Tsubasa imitates Sekai in order to dredge up Sensei's trauma, making him easier to manipulate.
Something occurred to me while I was putting together this post: it's possible that in all these cases the "cat" is a deliberate reference to Maya (the stray cat). The first one definitely is. The second one is in the context of Akira's past and how he might abuse a wizard, so a Maya reference makes total sense. The third one is less obvious, but Sensei's guilt over what he did to Maya is part of his trauma, so Tsubasa might bring that up along with the Sekai stuff. Of course this requires Tsubasa to know about Maya, but why not when she knows intimate details about his relationship with Sekai and has used her connections to investigate his past?

So why does "Sana" use the same phrase in this scene? Well, she says it in the middle of a discussion of other possible worlds where different girls end up with Akira, so maybe she wants him to think about a world where he ends up with Maya. On the face of it, it's kind of ridiculous that a reference so subtle could have any effect, but it might have worked: later that night, Sensei thinks about his conversation with Sana, and then almost immediately afterward he thinks about being with Maya instead of Ayane.

(That's not what she was doing, but he's rationalizing it that way so he can dismiss it.)
Maybe the roof scene was so traumatic that it primed him to think of Maya whenever he heard "cat got your tongue" from then on.

spoilers.title: Tsubasa theory: how and why
spoilers.html:
I'm going to throw out some guesses, but this is all very speculative. These probably weren't the most important concerns to Selebus - I'm guessing he started with what he wanted Sensei to hear, and only then figured out the most reasonable messenger and how to make it happen; he didn't start from an idea of Sana/Tsubasa/whoever wanting to say these things.

We know (or at least highly suspect) Tsubasa is a narrator (see post 1, post 2, post 3). As part of that role, she describes characters' thoughts, which means she can get inside their heads to at least some extent. As narrator she may be able to influence thoughts as well, such as when she spoke directly to Rin about a ticking clock and Rin heard it, or how she was the first to suggest the idea of Sensei becoming a god before he started thinking about it himself.

I admit there's a big leap between subconscious influence and total control of thoughts/speech, but there may be precedent for a narrator putting words in a girl's mouth: in "T is for Time" Makoto said some uncharacteristic things which echoed earlier narration. The other world's Sana could be even easier to influence since she's a clone.

During the time that Sensei and Ayane were in Himawari's world*, Tsubasa's body was apparently unconscious back in Kumon-mi, waiting to be killed and dismembered by Ami. But if you think about it, it's likely there's something more complex going on. The RAS's knowledge lets them stay awake during resets, so shouldn't the narrator who knows even more than them be able to do the same? Plus, we see Shiori preparing to reset Tsubasa, but we know she somehow avoids getting mind-wiped.

I had a thought: maybe Tsubasa is able to retain her memories because her mind isn't in her body when she gets reset. Sensei has the ability to mentally slip between worlds, ending up in the mind of another world's Akira. Maybe Tsubasa can do the same thing, but can enter minds other than just the other world's Tsubasa thanks to her narrator abilities.

[*] (off topic) I'm confused by the timeline: four months passed in Himawari's wish world. Himawari spent the same amount of time looking for her parents, so time wasn't moving faster there than the rest of the multiverse. But was Kumon-mi really in limbo for that long? I doubt Ami was rampaging for four months or that the corporation waited four months to send in a custodian to reset the world. And what was that whole deal with Himawari needing to keep her parents safe from a factory reset? What changed to prevent that?

So here is my extremely speculative theory of what happened:
  1. The reset starts. Tsubasa slips to Himawari's wish world, either because she knows Sensei will be there or just because she wants to learn more about her new ally (Himawari).
  2. Tsubasa seizes an oppurtunity to talk to Sensei through Sana, giving him cryptic hints so he doesn't become complacent in the idea of a monogamous future with Ayane. (Whatever Tsubasa's goals are, she's been throwing Tsukasa at Sensei to try and get him to embrace his inner predator. Himawari's wish is the antithesis to that.)
  3. Sensei returns to Kumon-mi and the custodians do their work. Shiori resets Tsubasa's body, but it's an empty vessel while her mind is elsewhere.
  4. After the custodians are finished, Tsubasa slips back into her restored body.
Of course, whether this would actually let her avoid the mind wipe depends on metaphysical questions about what it means to slip and whether your mind is still tied to your original brain. We don't have the answer to those, so it's at least possible.

One strike against this theory: it doesn't explain the adult Sana in "Four Letter Words" who recognizes Sensei and tells him she loves him. It would be cleaner if the two weird adult Sana scenes had the same explanation, but for now I don't see a way to tie them together.


I did briefly consider the possibility that it's Maya Prime speaking through Sana instead of Tsubasa, but in the "Infinite Joy" scene I can't see any reflection of Maya in her demeanor the way that I can with Tsubasa.

Tsubasa theory: how and why
I'm going to throw out some guesses, but this is all very speculative. These probably weren't the most important concerns to Selebus - I'm guessing he started with what he wanted Sensei to hear, and only then figured out the most reasonable messenger and how to make it happen; he didn't start from an idea of Sana/Tsubasa/whoever wanting to say these things.

). As part of that role, she describes characters' thoughts, which means she can get inside their heads to at least some extent. As narrator she may be able to influence thoughts as well, such as when she spoke directly to Rin about a ticking clock and Rin heard it, or how she was the first to suggest the idea of Sensei becoming a god before he started thinking about it himself.
I admit there's a big leap between subconscious influence and total control of thoughts/speech, but there may be precedent for a narrator putting words in a girl's mouth: in "T is for Time"
Makoto said some uncharacteristic things
which echoed earlier narration. The other world's Sana could be even easier to influence since she's a clone.
During the time that Sensei and Ayane were in Himawari's world*, Tsubasa's body was apparently unconscious back in Kumon-mi, waiting to be killed and dismembered by Ami. But if you think about it, it's likely there's something more complex going on. The RAS's knowledge lets them stay awake during resets, so shouldn't the narrator who knows even more than them be able to do the same? Plus, we see Shiori preparing to reset Tsubasa, but we know she somehow avoids getting mind-wiped.
I had a thought: maybe Tsubasa is able to retain her memories because her mind isn't in her body when she gets reset. Sensei has the ability to mentally slip between worlds, ending up in the mind of another world's Akira. Maybe Tsubasa can do the same thing, but can enter minds other than just the other world's Tsubasa thanks to her narrator abilities.
[*] (off topic)
I'm confused by the timeline: four months passed in Himawari's wish world. Himawari spent the same amount of time looking for her parents, so time wasn't moving faster there than the rest of the multiverse. But was Kumon-mi really in limbo for that long? I doubt Ami was rampaging for four months or that the corporation waited four months to send in a custodian to reset the world. And what was that whole deal with Himawari needing to keep her parents safe from a factory reset? What changed to prevent that?
So here is my extremely speculative theory of what happened:
The reset starts. Tsubasa slips to Himawari's wish world, either because she knows Sensei will be there or just because she wants to learn more about her new ally (Himawari).
Tsubasa seizes an oppurtunity to talk to Sensei through Sana, giving him cryptic hints so he doesn't become complacent in the idea of a monogamous future with Ayane. (Whatever Tsubasa's goals are, she's been throwing Tsukasa at Sensei to try and get him to embrace his inner predator. Himawari's wish is the antithesis to that.)
Sensei returns to Kumon-mi and the custodians do their work. Shiori resets Tsubasa's body, but it's an empty vessel while her mind is elsewhere.
After the custodians are finished, Tsubasa slips back into her restored body.
Of course, whether this would actually let her avoid the mind wipe depends on metaphysical questions about what it means to slip and whether your mind is still tied to your original brain. We don't have the answer to those, so it's at least possible.
One strike against this theory: it doesn't explain the adult Sana in "Four Letter Words" who recognizes Sensei and tells him she loves him. It would be cleaner if the two weird adult Sana scenes had the same explanation, but for now I don't see a way to tie them together.

spoilers.title: Tsubasa theory: how and why
spoilers.html:
I'm going to throw out some guesses, but this is all very speculative. These probably weren't the most important concerns to Selebus - I'm guessing he started with what he wanted Sensei to hear, and only then figured out the most reasonable messenger and how to make it happen; he didn't start from an idea of Sana/Tsubasa/whoever wanting to say these things.

We know (or at least highly suspect) Tsubasa is a narrator (see post 1, post 2, post 3). As part of that role, she describes characters' thoughts, which means she can get inside their heads to at least some extent. As narrator she may be able to influence thoughts as well, such as when she spoke directly to Rin about a ticking clock and Rin heard it, or how she was the first to suggest the idea of Sensei becoming a god before he started thinking about it himself.

I admit there's a big leap between subconscious influence and total control of thoughts/speech, but there may be precedent for a narrator putting words in a girl's mouth: in "T is for Time" Makoto said some uncharacteristic things which echoed earlier narration. The other world's Sana could be even easier to influence since she's a clone.

During the time that Sensei and Ayane were in Himawari's world*, Tsubasa's body was apparently unconscious back in Kumon-mi, waiting to be killed and dismembered by Ami. But if you think about it, it's likely there's something more complex going on. The RAS's knowledge lets them stay awake during resets, so shouldn't the narrator who knows even more than them be able to do the same? Plus, we see Shiori preparing to reset Tsubasa, but we know she somehow avoids getting mind-wiped.

I had a thought: maybe Tsubasa is able to retain her memories because her mind isn't in her body when she gets reset. Sensei has the ability to mentally slip between worlds, ending up in the mind of another world's Akira. Maybe Tsubasa can do the same thing, but can enter minds other than just the other world's Tsubasa thanks to her narrator abilities.

[*] (off topic) I'm confused by the timeline: four months passed in Himawari's wish world. Himawari spent the same amount of time looking for her parents, so time wasn't moving faster there than the rest of the multiverse. But was Kumon-mi really in limbo for that long? I doubt Ami was rampaging for four months or that the corporation waited four months to send in a custodian to reset the world. And what was that whole deal with Himawari needing to keep her parents safe from a factory reset? What changed to prevent that?

So here is my extremely speculative theory of what happened:
  1. The reset starts. Tsubasa slips to Himawari's wish world, either because she knows Sensei will be there or just because she wants to learn more about her new ally (Himawari).
  2. Tsubasa seizes an oppurtunity to talk to Sensei through Sana, giving him cryptic hints so he doesn't become complacent in the idea of a monogamous future with Ayane. (Whatever Tsubasa's goals are, she's been throwing Tsukasa at Sensei to try and get him to embrace his inner predator. Himawari's wish is the antithesis to that.)
  3. Sensei returns to Kumon-mi and the custodians do their work. Shiori resets Tsubasa's body, but it's an empty vessel while her mind is elsewhere.
  4. After the custodians are finished, Tsubasa slips back into her restored body.
Of course, whether this would actually let her avoid the mind wipe depends on metaphysical questions about what it means to slip and whether your mind is still tied to your original brain. We don't have the answer to those, so it's at least possible.

One strike against this theory: it doesn't explain the adult Sana in "Four Letter Words" who recognizes Sensei and tells him she loves him. It would be cleaner if the two weird adult Sana scenes had the same explanation, but for now I don't see a way to tie them together.

I did briefly consider the possibility that it's Maya Prime speaking through Sana instead of Tsubasa, but in the "Infinite Joy" scene I can't see any reflection of Maya in her demeanor the way that I can with Tsubasa.

spoilers.title: Tsubasa theory: how and why
spoilers.html:
I'm going to throw out some guesses, but this is all very speculative. These probably weren't the most important concerns to Selebus - I'm guessing he started with what he wanted Sensei to hear, and only then figured out the most reasonable messenger and how to make it happen; he didn't start from an idea of Sana/Tsubasa/whoever wanting to say these things.

We know (or at least highly suspect) Tsubasa is a narrator (see post 1, post 2, post 3). As part of that role, she describes characters' thoughts, which means she can get inside their heads to at least some extent. As narrator she may be able to influence thoughts as well, such as when she spoke directly to Rin about a ticking clock and Rin heard it, or how she was the first to suggest the idea of Sensei becoming a god before he started thinking about it himself.

I admit there's a big leap between subconscious influence and total control of thoughts/speech, but there may be precedent for a narrator putting words in a girl's mouth: in "T is for Time" Makoto said some uncharacteristic things which echoed earlier narration. The other world's Sana could be even easier to influence since she's a clone.

During the time that Sensei and Ayane were in Himawari's world*, Tsubasa's body was apparently unconscious back in Kumon-mi, waiting to be killed and dismembered by Ami. But if you think about it, it's likely there's something more complex going on. The RAS's knowledge lets them stay awake during resets, so shouldn't the narrator who knows even more than them be able to do the same? Plus, we see Shiori preparing to reset Tsubasa, but we know she somehow avoids getting mind-wiped.

I had a thought: maybe Tsubasa is able to retain her memories because her mind isn't in her body when she gets reset. Sensei has the ability to mentally slip between worlds, ending up in the mind of another world's Akira. Maybe Tsubasa can do the same thing, but can enter minds other than just the other world's Tsubasa thanks to her narrator abilities.

[*] (off topic) I'm confused by the timeline: four months passed in Himawari's wish world. Himawari spent the same amount of time looking for her parents, so time wasn't moving faster there than the rest of the multiverse. But was Kumon-mi really in limbo for that long? I doubt Ami was rampaging for four months or that the corporation waited four months to send in a custodian to reset the world. And what was that whole deal with Himawari needing to keep her parents safe from a factory reset? What changed to prevent that?

So here is my extremely speculative theory of what happened:
  1. The reset starts. Tsubasa slips to Himawari's wish world, either because she knows Sensei will be there or just because she wants to learn more about her new ally (Himawari).
  2. Tsubasa seizes an oppurtunity to talk to Sensei through Sana, giving him cryptic hints so he doesn't become complacent in the idea of a monogamous future with Ayane. (Whatever Tsubasa's goals are, she's been throwing Tsukasa at Sensei to try and get him to embrace his inner predator. Himawari's wish is the antithesis to that.)
  3. Sensei returns to Kumon-mi and the custodians do their work. Shiori resets Tsubasa's body, but it's an empty vessel while her mind is elsewhere.
  4. After the custodians are finished, Tsubasa slips back into her restored body.
Of course, whether this would actually let her avoid the mind wipe depends on metaphysical questions about what it means to slip and whether your mind is still tied to your original brain. We don't have the answer to those, so it's at least possible.

One strike against this theory: it doesn't explain the adult Sana in "Four Letter Words" who recognizes Sensei and tells him she loves him. It would be cleaner if the two weird adult Sana scenes had the same explanation, but for now I don't see a way to tie them together.
View attachment 5476951 View attachment 5476952 View attachment 5476954

I did briefly consider the possibility that it's Maya Prime speaking through Sana instead of Tsubasa, but in the "Infinite Joy" scene I can't see any reflection of Maya in her demeanor the way that I can with Tsubasa.

That's a very loaded and leading question. I'm assuming the reaction would be to have sex with them or not? Well, I wouldn't have sex with any minors, officer. Thank you very much.
That being said, I think a more reasonable scenario would be: "Would you indulge in your partner's attempt to connect with you through sex, even though she's terrified of it - or will you reassure her that you won't ask that of her, even though you feel that if it doesn't happen, you'll eventually break up?"

Because I think that, if we take the LiL nonsense/drama out of the situation, what we're presented with is a dude that needs to have sex in a relationship, and a partner that is trying to bridge that gap. Anything could happen, tbh. Maybe the dude doesn't really need sex in his life. Maybe the partner is able to cope and heal. Maybe (and most likely) they'll just split with or without this one experience - because in the real world dealbreakers are a thing, and the sad reality of the situation is that people with mental traumas are often just too much work.

Because I think that, if we take the LiL nonsense/drama out of the situation, what we're presented with is a dude that needs to have sex in a relationship, and a partner that is trying to bridge that gap. Anything could happen, tbh. Maybe the dude doesn't really need sex in his life. Maybe the partner is able to cope and heal. Maybe (and most likely) they'll just split with or without this one experience - because in the real world dealbreakers are a thing, and the sad reality of the situation is that people with mental traumas are often just too much work.
